utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May I have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, David Re, Senior Trial Attorney; accompanied by the Prosecutor, Madam Del Ponte; trial attorneys Mr. Gilles Dutertre, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Nisha Valabhji, Ms. Katrina Gustafson; and case manager to my left, Mr. Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. For the Defence. First the Haradinaj Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ben Emmerson, lead counsel for Mr. Haradinaj; together with Rodney Dixon, Susan Park, assisted today by Mr. Michael O'Reilly and Mr. Andrew Strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. For the Balaj Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Gregor Guy-Smith, appearing on behalf of Idriz Balaj, with co-counsel Colleen Rohan and assisted Natalie van Den Berge, Bart Willemsen, Aurelie Roche, and Joeri Maas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. And finally for the Brahimaj Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Richard Harvey for Lahi Brahimaj; with me, Mr. Paul Troop, that's my co-counsel; and we're assisted by our case manager, Ms. Antoniette Trapani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Mr. Haradinaj, can you hear me in a language you understand? I did not receive -- THE ACCUSED HARADINAJ: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be ever any moment when translation is not functioning properly, would you please inform us. And then, Mr. Balaj, same question for you. THE ACCUSED BALAJ: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask to turn on the mike, please, we can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please turn on the microphone; otherwise, the interpreters cannot hear you. So the same question for you, Mr. Balaj. THE ACCUSED BALAJ: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I can follow it completely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then finally, Mr. Brahimaj, same question for you. And could you please turn on the microphone -- I see it's on already. Yes. THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also can hear me in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ: [Interpretation] I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever you would have any difficulties in following the proceedings, please tell us immediately. THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Today is the opening of the trial, but before opening the trial, I'd like to make a few small observations and remarks. First of all, Mr. Re, I'm addressing you that it seems that the exhibits and the list of exhibits that will be presented in evidence, that the distribution of that is not going smooth yet. May I invite you to pay specific attention to that element so that everyone in this courtroom is able to prepare properly for the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I hear Your Honour. We're concentrating on the first witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then another matter, just to make sure that everyone is aware of that. The Chamber received this morning a motion filed by the Defence for the exclusion of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll deal with the matter, not before the opening statement, but we'll deal with the matter as soon as possible. And, of course, the function of the exclusion of evidence, of course, is different in the different systems. To keep matters away from the jury is not exactly the same as Judges reading the material which is supposed to be excluded, but we'll deal with the matter as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then next item I'd like to draw attention to is, Mr. Re, it seems that witness protection pre-trial has been dealt with in the normal way, but there's still a few lacunas in terms of protection of witnesses during trial. I take it that you will, without any further delay, will pay attention to that. Yes. Then finally, some concerns have been expressed last Friday by you, Mr. Guy-Smith, on opening statements, who would deliver it, what happened on the Popovic case. I oriented myself and I notice at this moment that in the Popovic case, the main issue in the beginning was whether, when the Prosecutor was addressing the Chamber, whether that was part of the opening statement and whether that opening statement was supposed to be delivered in July or, rather, in August. That's a rather procedural matter which is -- which does not in any way apply here, I would say. An opening statement is there to give an outline to, may I say, the trier of fact - usually, of course, it's the jury - an outline of what the Prosecution's case will be. The parties have, well, a wide discretion in formulating the opening statement, the evidence to be presented as they wish, and the Chamber, of course, there's no need to start every sentence by saying, "The evidence will show that," because that would not only be boring but be repetitious as well. But I think that everyone is fully aware of what an opening statement is. I would like to add to that that where, in strict jury systems, an opening statement is really limited to facts and nothing else, and, of course, an opening statement here addresses the Chamber, the Chamber who is not only a trier of fact, but also deals with legal matters. So where it's of no use to address the jury with legal matters in an opening statement, that might be different here. I take it that, everyone being at a high professional level, is fully aware of what is expected at this stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm grateful for your comments, Your Honour, and believe that we do all understand the purpose of an opening statement. My concern, as expressed before, was the question of whether or not it was going to be used as a bully pulpit for a political speech, but I trust --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not see, and certainly not on the basis of the Popovic example, that there would be any reason to express such concern prior to hearing what the Prosecution is saying in its opening statement. I also urge the parties, which is, from what I understand, quite common not to object or intervene unless really necessary. After having given this guidance, I'd like to declare this trial open and give the opportunity to the Prosecution to address the Chamber in its opening statement. Madam Prosecutor, I see that you're on your feet, so I take it that you'll at least start with the opening statement. Please proceed. MS. DEL PONTE: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. This case is about crimes in Kosovo in 1998. But although this trial takes place against the background of historic negotiation in 2007 to decide the future of Kosovo, I am not - I am not - here to make a political address. These proceedings have no connection with any wider diplomatic events. My office takes no part in those matters and has no involvement in them. This is a criminal trial, and I have indicted the accused before you on the merits of the case, on the facts. The three men come before you accused of crimes - ugly, cruel, and violent crimes; crimes of murder, deportation, torture, rape, abduction, forced imprisonment, and the most brutal assault; crimes that took place out of sight, away from the eyes of international observers or monitors. Be in no doubt, as the Prosecution will prove, that these men - this warlord with his lieutenant and his jailer - have blood on their hands. And it is the blood of innocent civilians, victims who did not support the accused or the cause of the KLA; victims who were very often alone and vulnerable, and who were systematically targeted, abducted, murdered and made to vanish. If these accused had had their way, their victims would never have been seen again. They would have been simply swallowed up among the other horrors of this conflict and would quite literally have sunk without a trace in the silent waters of Lake Radonjic, in the inner reaches of the Dukagjin Zone. But the murdered victims in this case did not disappear. Their bodies and their stories have been uncovered, and in the weeks that follow, as the evidence emerges, they will speak to you in their own way from their graves. The voices of those who were last seen in KLA hands, whose bodies remain undiscovered or unidentified, will be heard through the anguished voices of their grieving loved ones. The voices of some of those who were tortured and brutalised by the KLA will be heard directly in the courtroom. There may not be many such voices, for this is not a case, like others, that deal with mass exterminations and thousands of deaths. We will not be able to bring before this Court evidence of all the crimes that were committed in this part of Kosovo. That would be impossible. But as each day of this trial passes, as each witness is examined and each document produced, I am sure the Chamber will begin to penetrate the closed world of the Dukagjin Zone, which was the heartland of the Haradinaj clan, in the centre of Ramush Haradinaj's power base. Perhaps also, as in no other case, geography will be the key to understanding the facts. Geography itself is another of the silent witnesses in this case, and I would urge the Trial Chamber to pay particular attention to the locations, the distances, the scale of the activities, and the accessibility of the places that will feature in the events. I would even encourage the Trial Chamber, at a suitable point in the trial, to make a site visit to crime scenes so that you can see these places for yourselves. I make no apology; this will not be an easy prosecution. It is a prosecution, frankly, that some did not want to see brought, and that few supported by their cooperation at both international and local level. But I insisted on this prosecution, and I bring it with the confidence that the Trial Chamber will find the Prosecution evidence compelling and convincing. The protection of witnesses who have had the courage to come forward has been, and will continue to be, of critical importance. You know that many witnesses are reluctant to testify. Some are even terrified. The intimidation and threats suffered by witnesses in this case has been a serious ongoing problem for the individuals concerned and for this Prosecution. This problem has not gone away. Witnesses continue to receive threats, both veiled and direct. Just this weekend, our first direct victim witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that the statements now are not only highly prejudicial but go well outside the purpose of any opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Del Ponte, it is mainly understood that -- just to give an example, that where the witnesses are well -- are going to tell the truth or not, that's an evaluation already of -- what will happen is not appropriate during an opening statement. I wonder whether -- of course, this Chamber will have to decide on -- it has not decided yet, as I mentioned before, on matters of witness protection, and of course we'll hear, I take it, from the Prosecution the need for such protection. If no further detail would be needed in relation to the reluctance of witnesses to testify, and that's one of the problems you encountered in preparing this -- preparing this case, then I would suggest that we proceed with hearing from you what the evidence will bring us, unless you would disagree with me and then I'd like to hear you. MS. DEL PONTE: Mr. President, I'm just informing the Court that this weekend - that this weekend - I received an information about threats that a witness have received now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that that's -- MS. DEL PONTE: So I wonder why I could not inform the Court about an event, about the facts that occurred during the weekend and it's directly related with this trial. Because, Mr. President, if I have no witnesses appearing in court, I will be obliged to withdraw this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I think there's nothing inappropriate informing the Court about threats. But whether, at the opening statement, where in general terms you have set out that this is of major concern to the Prosecution, whether to go into any further details, where we'll not be able to further inquire into the matter, whether that would be the best course is subject to doubt. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber invites you to proceed. MS. DEL PONTE: The Chamber has already granted protective measures to more than a third of our witnesses. I know that you understand and appreciate the difficulties that witnesses face in testifying against these accused. But what I want to say, Mr. President, is that I have full confidence that you will take every possible measure to allow the witnesses to travel to The Hague to testify safely and to allow the truth to be heard. Your Honours, there was nothing noble or heroic about the crimes in this case. There was nothing patriotic or virtuous about them. They were brutal and bloody murders. The three accused were gangster in uniform and in control, and as the Trial Chamber will see, that prove to be a sinister and deadly combination for the victims in this case. Thank you, President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Prosecutor. May I take it that Mr. Re will continue the opening statement? MS. DEL PONTE: Yes, Mr. President, with your authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Re, you are invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: With the words of the Prosecutor in the Court's ears, nothing noble, heroic, patriotic, or virtuous about the crimes that were committed by the accused. The crimes charged against these accused arise out of the tragic events in Kosovo in 1998. It was a war in which crimes too numerous to detail were committed against innocent civilians by both sides to the conflict. These were crimes that resulted ultimately in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic; crimes that put on trial other members of his government, including his Prime Minister; and other generals in another court as we sit here today. They were crimes that resulted in the conviction of a KLA member before this Tribunal for torture, murder, cruel treatment, in a KLA prison camp in which that Trial Chamber, the Limaj Trial Chamber, found that there was "quite a culture of violence in that prison camp." Well, that was a culture of violence which pervaded the area under the control of these accused before this Court today. In that brutal conflict, both Serbs and Albanians, both sides, committed war crimes. The crimes charged here in this court involved acts of unspeakable brutality against an innocent civilian population, a population targeted by the accused and their KLA associates, either for not supporting the KLA or merely - merely - for the perception of not supporting the KLA. Alleged collaborators were shown absolutely no mercy. They were driven from their homes, they were driven from their villages, they were abducted, they were held at the point of a gun against their will, they were tortured in prison camps under KLA control. These accused sitting in this court committed despicable crimes against humanity; they committed serious war crimes. They committed these crimes as part of a joint criminal enterprise to consolidate control over a small part of northern Kosovo; this area is known as the Dukagjin Zone. Your Honours will hear a lot about this particular zone in this trial. I'll display it on the overhead for Your Honours' benefit. The first map is the Times map of the Balkans in which you can see Kosovo. We'll move down Kosovo itself to the -- Your Honours can see on the map, the map of Kosovo. The northern part is the Dukagjin. Next slide. You can see the length of it on red on the left is about 100 kilometres in width, and you can compare that on the map on the right to that of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, may -- I expect that you'll later on present these maps in evidence so that they -- or do they need any marking for identification at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it's part of the opening. I can certainly present them in evidence at a later point they're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I expect that you're referring to matters that you'll later introduce into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then, if none of the parties disagrees, then I'd like not to have exhibited it at this moment, just to be illustrative material.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next map is labeled "Dukagjin Operative Zone," and that was accused Haradinaj's area of responsibility zone. You can see the blue part on the left, which shows it against the Albanian and Montenegrin border and dissecting the left-hand third of Kosovo. Moving to the next slide, there's a red place in the middle, and that is the are under the total KLA control of Haradinaj. If you put it in the next slide, you can see it in another map which shows an overhead of Kosovo. Now, a military campaign in which these accused indulged is not illegal under international law, but the means by which the accused consolidated their control most certainly was; and that is, Your Honour, why they sit here today. The result of their military campaign of fear, violence, and persecution between March and September 1998 was 48 murder victims, of which 35 bodies have been recovered; 13 of these were found in a small area along the Lake Radonjic canal, less than 1 and a half kilometres from the home of Ramush Haradinaj in Gllogjan; 8 bodies remain unidentified; 13 of the victims disappeared without trace in KLA custody; 29 of the victims were tortured while in KLA custody; one woman was raped by the accused Balaj, who sits in court today; 35 victims were abducted. The villages were, to use the term which has become known in the media, cleansed of their non-KLA-supporting inhabitants. These were mainly Kosovo Serbs and Roma. By the end of April 1998, almost no Serbs remained in the villages in Haradinaj's Dukagjin Zone. Their houses and properties were destroyed and Orthodox churches, cemeteries and tombstones were desecrated. 123 Serb families lived there in January 1998; the last couple, the last Serb couple, an elderly one, left on the 5th of May, 1998, when KLA soldiers came to their house and told them that they belonged -- the area belonged to Albanians and they, the Serbs, should go to Serbia. They did. But who are these accused? Who are the accused sitting in the court today? The three accused are primary members - the primary members - the most important participants in the joint criminal enterprise charged by the Prosecutor. They were all very important members of the KLA, that's the Kosovo Liberation Army, or the Ushtria Clirimtare e Kosoves, or the UCK, UCK, in the Dukagjin area. As early as November 1997, a communique published by the KLA used these chilling words: "Every collaborator whom in this form or that causes harm to the Albanian nation is to suffer." For the purposes of this opening, I'm not going to detail or go into any detail on the law. I will only briefly say that they were members of the joint criminal enterprise; it's pleaded in the indictment. It's set out in great detail in our pre-trial brief filed on the 29th of January. Your Honours know the law; I don't need to trouble you with the law. But I will remind you of the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise that is pleaded, and that was to violently suppress any form of perceived opposition to the KLA within the Dukagjin Zone; to allow the KLA to control its total control -- consolidate its control over that area. Those in this joint criminal enterprise or those used by its participants sought to expel, either by force or threat of force, all Serb civilians from the area. As I said before, they did this by armed attacks, abductions, torture, and ultimately by the ultimate sanction of murder. The participants to this joint criminal enterprise worked to suppress any form of perceived or potential collaboration with the Serbian authorities or opposition to the KLA members by the civilian population. They did this by violently targeting perceived collaborators and opponents in a manner intended both to stifle opposition to the KLA and to allow the KLA to control the general population through a campaign of intimidation, fear, and violence. The campaign, as I said, lasted from March to September 1998, and during this time the non-KLA-supporting residents of the Dukagjin Zone, in this small area of Kosovo, which Your Honours saw on the map a moment ago, lived in fear of their lives. Ramush Haradinaj, known as Smajl, was born in 1968. He became a commander of the zone in February 1998 upon his return to Kosovo to participate in the struggle against the Serbian authorities. As the commander in that zone, he was by far the most powerful and important individual in that zone. He was aware of what was going on in the zone. He received regular reports from his subcommanders. Such was his power that he controlled who could enter his territory, as well as movement within his territory; he organised, he planned, he personally led KLA operations. He appointed subcommanders and officers. He assigned soldiers and duties to -- soldiers and units to duties within the area. He established local village headquarters. He issued orders to officers, to local village commanders. He issued orders to the general population. He ordered mobilisations. He created brigades. He appointed brigade commanders. He personally controlled the collection and distribution of arms and supplies within the zone. He organised military training. He himself took responsibility for disciplinary and financial matters, including collecting and distributing funds throughout the zone. He established an army within that zone. He was a member of the KLA's General Staff. He, Haradinaj, personally prohibited all political activity on the basis that, due to wartime conditions, the KLA was the responsible authority within the Dukagjin Zone. Such was his control over what went on in that zone that Haradinaj himself took control over civilian affairs within that zone. As an example, a list of duties he sent to village headquarters included supplying the general population, registering births and deaths in the village, ensuring the rational use of "national resources," and even down to the minor details of assisting the population in sowing and harvesting crops. The breadth of his power between March and September 1998 was consistent with his stated goal of "bringing war to the people." At the time of his indictment, he was the Prime Minister of Kosovo. Idriz Balaj goes by the nickname of Toger, or Togeri, meaning lieutenant. He was born in 1971. During the indictment period he commanded a special unit called the Black Eagles; it was based in the small village of Rznic, or Irzniq, according to the Serb or Albanian name. It had between 40 and 100 members. Haradinaj helped to train the Black Eagles. Balaj was directly subordinated to Haradinaj. Who were these Black Eagles? The Black Eagles were notorious throughout the zone for their brutality. They were notorious because Haradinaj gave them free reign to operate throughout the zone. The Black Eagles abducted, imprisoned, tortured, and murdered non-KLA-supporting civilians. Balaj, as its commander, operated with absolute impunity. He was a law unto himself in the Dukagjin Zone. He carried with him a notebook. The notebook contained the names of "wanted persons." The wanted persons were people that Balaj was looking for because they opposed the KLA in some manner or another, or were perceived to be opposing the KLA. The bodies of 43 such people were found along a stretch of canal less than 2 kilometres from his headquarters, a stretch of canal which goes through the village in which his headquarters were located. That area, that stretch of canal, was known locally at the time, and for very good reason, as the Black Eagles' execution site. In September 1998, the bodies of some 20 victims were found directly next to the execution site, next to a section of the wall, the canal wall, riddled with bullet-holes. Cartridges were found next to the bodies - and I'll come to that a little later in my opening - and a number of bodies were found floating nearby in the canal. After the cessation of hostilities, Balaj became a major in the Kosovo Protection Corps. Balaj himself, in his own diary, which I'll display on the board -- of the rote of the period before April 1998 -- can Your Honours read what's displayed on the overhead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If something is put on the ELMO, then we can read it, but -- well, at this moment it's, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was just a little clearer than my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear. That's e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In e-court, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The e-court button, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He wrote: "Of the period before 14 April 1998, during this period, I," Balaj, "thought that the Special Unit could operate within the framework of the zone to help the country so we could damage the enemy. With the help of Commander Ramush Haradinaj, the opportunity existed and a request was granted for the creation of the Special Unit known as the Black Eagles. It was formed on the 14th of April, 1998, in the village of Gllogjan. In each village I assembled some lads and trained them for the Special Unit with the help of Commander Ramush." He then goes on to say: "It had between 40 and 100 soldiers and it undertook many operations in the villages named." In his own pre-trial brief, Haradinaj says of the Black Eagles, they were a group of KLA soldiers whose function was to provide military support to the armed Kosovar Albanian resistance and to mount attacks on Serb military positions and personnel. They were deployed often in small combat units across the zone and outside it. What, of course, he doesn't mention is the fact that these were the Black Eagles who were taking abducted Serbs, and those who did serve and oppose the KLA, to an execution site by the side of the canal and shooting them. Lahi Brahimaj, also known as Maxhup, which is Albanian for gypsy, was born in 1970. On the 23rd of June, 1998, he was appointed the deputy commander of the Dukagjin Zone, and after became a high-ranking member of the Kosovo Protection Corps. His role in this indictment is mainly connected with the operation of the KLA's notorious detention centre in Jablanica. On the screen in front of you, you will see what is now the wreck of a farm building outside of Jablanica, which was where he established his detention facility. You can see it on the right of the screen, the remains of the building in which he had his office, and underneath it there is a basement in which the prisoners were kept. The basement was often full of water. The other accused, Haradinaj and Balaj, regularly visited the prison. It was in that prison that the KLA tortured, mistreated, and ultimately murdered many of the victims, the bodies of which were found along the Radonjic Canal. Brahimaj himself lived about 1 kilometre -- his headquarters were about 1 kilometre from the prison. An armed conflict is necessary for the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. From at least the 24th of March, 1998, there was an armed conflict in Kosovo, and in particular in this part of Kosovo, the part relevant to the indictment. Now, why do we choose that date? That date is significant to this case because it was on that date that Serbian military and MUP forces attacked the Haradinaj family compound in Glodjane, and it was from that date that Haradinaj was the undisputed commander of his zone. Now, the Defence pre-trial briefs make something of the fact that the Limaj case, the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 134, that before the end of May 1998, the KLA sufficiently possessed the characteristics of an organised group able to engage in an internal armed conflict. Now, the Defence do not want the Trial Chamber -- they do not want the Court to find an armed conflict before that date; that is, before the end of May 1998. However, the Limaj case was very different to this particular case before the Trial Chamber. The crimes charged were in a different zone. You'll see in e-court now the crimes -- you will see the crimes, the area charged was in the Lapusnik zone and for murders in Berisha. If we just go back to the entire one, you can see on the left of the map is the Dukagjin Zone and on the right of the map is the Limaj -- is the Limaj area. So you can see when you look at the two together, they are entirely distinct zones and there is absolutely no conflict between the Limaj Trial Chamber making a finding in relation to an indictment confined to a later period and Your Honours finding an armed conflict existing on an earlier -- in an earlier period. In fact, the Serbian authorities had no doubt that they were engaged in an armed conflict from that earlier date, and I will demonstrate that a little later. Indeed, Haradinaj himself made no secret of the fact, or at least before he was indicted for war crimes, that the armed conflict existed before the end of May 1998. On the 5th of September, 2001, several years before he was indicted, he was interviewed by a Swiss journalist. He told her, and you will see on the display in e-court, "where was your base? I think you can tell me this. What was your base during the war?" And he said, "Pec Decane, Djakovica, up until the region of Klina. I was there the whole time. From March 1998 until June 1999, 15 months" - yes, that's 15 months - "of open warfare. I was there face to face," I underline that, "face to face with the Serbs." Now, those aren't the words of a man who was not engaged in an armed conflict in March, April, and May 1998. In his own book, while describing the military attack, the Serbian military attack on his house or the family compound in Glodjane, he said -- this is in relation to an attack in Prekaze. "After what happened in Prekaz, Likoshan, and Qirez we, in the Dukagjin zone, did not sit twiddling our thumbs." Just highlight the bottom part. "Serbian forces were continually attacking everywhere, day and night, and totally in the open. Serbia saw the danger of the war spreading, and, of course, also saw the war coming very close to the border. At the same time, we had started preparations for more direct action with open attacks and open war. I believe that the Serbs knew that Jabllanice was a flash-point for the war." Those are in his own words. Also in his own words, in his own book, when asked about the attack, Haradinaj said -- when describing the attack, he said: "I knew that something would happen after Gllogjan was built up. The events of March 24th happened almost without any consequences, and when we started, we knew that neither side would give up its ambitions." I pause there. "Neither side." An armed conflict requires two sides. Haradinaj there, in his own book, is describing the fact that there were two sides to the conflict in March 1998. "So you had to work, or be wiped out. My first idea was for Gllogjan not to be the front line. This should be at least one village further on, so that we would have a base behind the lines. To wage a war, you have to have a base of this kind to give you room to prepare operations, for soldiers to rest, et cetera. So we worked hard to take equipment as fast as possible to the villages where the enemy would come, such as Irzniq, Baballoq, Gramacel, and Shaptej. We then extended the firing line as far as Rastavica. Seeing that we were expanding, Serbia also worked hard but not to destroy us, and solely with the idea of taking certain positions as close to us as possible, to hem us in until the day when they would strike back." Now, retired Yugoslav army general, Dragan Jovanovic, who was in the field for the entire period of the indictment and commanded the 125th Motorised Brigade of the Yugoslav Army, from the 12th of June onwards, will testify that on the -- will testify in this court that on the 28th of February, 1998, KLA soldiers, that his soldiers, as part of an organised group, attacked a Serbian Ministry of the Interior - that's what we call in this Court MUP - patrol in the village of Likosane. Jovanovic will tell the Court it was from then, the 28th of February, 1998, that the VJ, the Yugoslav Army, realised that the KLA was militarily organising itself and getting trained. KLA incidents with the VJ and the MUP, that is, the combined Serbian forces, continued from then onwards. As an example, I'll display on the screen an order or a report dated the 23rd of February, 1998, entitled "Military Secret - Confidential" and signed by Colonel, now General, Bozidar Delic, who will also testify in this Court, and he said: "In the last months of 1997, but especially January 1998, there has been a significant deterioration in the political and security situation in the territory of Djakovica municipality," and he describes an area which is the Dukagjin Zone, the area -- or partly the Dukagjin Zone. The area has a total surface of 90 square kilometres, and the villages which are leading in extremism are the villages of Jablanica, Kraljane, Zabelj, Grgoc." Underneath that, he wrote: "According to what we have learnt, this territory has not been under the control of the Republic of Serbia organs since several years ago. As the Crmljane police department withdrew, the territory was fully abandoned for years, only to fall under the control of the separatists and terrorists of the so-called KLA in 1997." A KLA communique issued on the 11th of March, 1998, referred to a conflict, clashes between Serbian military and KLA fighters. It said: "In the last few days since 7th of March, our armed forces have clashed on a broad front, with formations of the occupying Serbian military and police forces and Chetnik volunteers. Military confrontations stretch across a wide front, extending from Gllogoc in the direction of Skender in the north, towards Kline, Mitrovice in the east, and the villages along the Cicavice ridge from Gllogoc in the direction of Prishtina including many villages in the Drenica village -- Drenica region. Underneath that, the UCK, that's the KLA's military formations also engaged occupation forces," that's the Serbs, in the "Llap region, in the area between Decan, Gjakove, and Kline, and between Malisheve and Rahovec crossing from the Lumihat region. There were also engagements on a line stretching from Decane to Pec." And underneath that: "The UCK fought the invader's forces and succeeded in breaking through the enemy's lines on several fronts against police and military sieges, inflicting heavy losses on the enemy's military, police, and volunteer forces and considerable material damage." That was contemporaneous with a report written by General Delic, who -- again, he will testify in this court, on the 5th of March, talking about his, the 549th Motorised Brigade's area of responsibility. And he said: "What is characteristic about these events is the fact that an escalation of terrorist activity has taken place," meaning the KLA, "widening the area of operations of the terrorist groups in the area of Jablanica. We estimate that the attacks on the Serbian population in the villages of Bec, Crmljane, and Ratis, will be followed by attacks on the remaining Serbs in the villages of Bites, Janos, Ljug Bunar, and Vranic. We believe that the terrorists' primary objective in these attacks was not killing Serbs but creating panic, abandoning property, and moving out of Kosovo. It seems that this objective will be accomplished to a great extent." Well, those were certainly prescient words because that is exactly what happened. On the 22nd of April, 1998, Colonel Lazarevic of the Pristina Corps reported to a commander of a terrorist attack, in which he describes 20 or 30 terrorists," which of course indicates an organised force, "launching an infantry attack on a section of units of the 52nd Military Police Battalion. At the time we had information from the MUP that three tractors carrying weapons were travelling from Bec, and we believe they were travelling in the area of Jablanica. The attack lasted approximately 30 minutes." Another indication of the military conflict that was occurring at the time is in a daily report sent on the 3rd of May, 1998, in relation to an attack on that day by "Albanian terrorists on a MUP patrol near Djakovica, near Panosevac village, which they say, "following this village, synchronised mortar fire was opened from the surrounding villages at the MUP check-point located on the Panosevac village." On the 9th of May, the commander of the 549th Brigade reported that because of the activity of terrorist gangs on the main road, Pristina-Klina-Pec-Djakovica, an order had to be issued, it was a very serious order in military terms, an order one says: "Until further notice, I forbid movement of all military vehicles and civilian vehicles transporting members of the corps along the Pristina-Klina-Pec and the Pristina-Klina-Djakovica roads." It went further. On the 12th of May, General Pavkovic issued an order in the Pristina Corps, again referring to the activities of terrorist gangs, and both General Delic and General Zivanovic will tell the Court that this was referring to -- they received these orders. This was referring to the KLA, organised KLA activities. This order was more serious. Such was the deterioration of the situation as of the 12th of May that order number 1 said: "Until further notice, I prohibit any movement of army vehicles and civilian vehicles belonging to army officers and civilians employed by the army used for driving members of the corps on those main roads." General Zivanovic and General Delic will tell the Court that the Serbian military and Ministry of the Interior forces suffered continual attacks, organised attacks, by KLA forces in that period before the period in which the Limaj Trial Chamber found an armed conflict existed in Kosovo. In fact, the KLA, in issuing a communique on the 13th of May, was likewise of the view, as the Prosecution is, that an armed conflict was occurring in May in that particular territory, particular area. And they describe the period during March, April, and the first part of May, "the Albanian people's struggle against the Serbian invade had continued and grew stronger under the leadership of the KLA. On the orders of the UCK/KLA General Staff, successive organised operations against the invasion troops," that is, the VJ and the MUP, "were carried out in Operational Zone 1, that is, the operational subzones of Drenica, Erenik, Dukagjin, Pastrik, and Llap." They then say: "In the course of bitter fighting on the front, the invading forces carried out major human and material losses. Throughout this --" and chillingly, chillingly, the next line said: "Throughout this period, operations were also carried out against Albanian collaborationists who, despite earlier warnings, did not abandon their anti-national courses of action." In the subzone of Erenik, several successive operations were carried out against the invader in Glodjane, Baballoq, and Hulaj. Our forces," that is KLA, "waged a bitter struggle against the enemy," that's the VJ and MUP, "throughout the period. Our army" - army - "has broken the enemy's attacks and is continuing successfully to fight and defend the liberated areas." Zivanovic will testify that on the 23rd of May, KLA soldiers mounted such an attack upon his -- that is, Zivanovic's force, in the Djakovica-Panosevac road, that he, Zivanovic, needed to deploy 200 soldiers to secure the border area. In military terms, 200 soldiers is a lot of manpower. The attacks continued throughout June and July. Zivanovic will enforce that the road from Djakovica to Junik was dangerous for military convoys and they were frequently attacked. Haradinaj himself, in minutes of his own headquarters in Glodjane, in handwritten minutes dated the 13th of June, 1998, referred to a front line situation beyond the highway up to Voksh and Pobergj. In the minutes of his agenda held on the 21st of June, 1998, demonstrating his control, it read -- the minutes of the meeting read: "The meeting as all present agreed aims to reach agreement on the systemisation, organisation, and coordination of activities in these areas." The activities were the planning operations against Serbia on a wider scale in the Dukagjin area, a coordinated defence from Serbian offensive and attacks, deployment of manpower, technical equipment in specific areas at a specific time, division of operation subzones in the region, timely information in time on the development of combat attacks and defence, joint meetings of the operational HQ, a joint fight against the enemy's intelligence and counter-intelligence, and a joint fight against evil-doers, criminals, rule-breakers in the free zones, et cetera. Showing the organised nature of Haradinaj's Dukagjin Zone staff are the minutes of the 23rd of June, 1998, in which the staff of the Dukagjin Zone are set out. The commander is Ramush Haradinaj. The deputy commander is Lahi Brahimaj. Going down, you can see responsible for sabotage and anti-terrorist activities is Togeri, the lieutenant, that's Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On the 24th of June, 1998, Haradinaj issued an order. It was a very important order. The order was "to carry out a general mobilisation of human and material resources" in his area. Part 2 of the order says -- it was expressed to be "to properly prepare the population, combatants, and military officers for the needs of war." Number 4 says: "To take measures to prevent any activity that goes to the detriment of our war." And this order is one which the Prosecution will be relying upon in the course of the trial. The measures which he specified or didn't set out there to prevent any activity that goes to the detriment of our war goes to the heart of the joint criminal enterprise charged, because the measures Haradinaj and the people acting pursuant to the joint criminal enterprise took went far beyond anything which could legitimately be used under the laws of war. In this court, MUP officers will testify. The MUP had a slightly different approach to the VJ. They will tell you of frequent attacks. A senior officer in Serbian intelligence, who had access to the highest level of surveillance of the accused and the KLA, will testify here that, in their view, the real start of the armed uprising of the KLA was in January 1998; that attacks carried out by the KLA against the police, the army, the Serbs, other non-Albanians, and loyal Albanians were carried out on a daily basis; that the KLA carried out, during the indictment period, synchronised attacks throughout the zone. Another MUP officer will tell this Court that from spring 1998, the KLA increased the number of ambushes and attacks on the MUP, the VJ, and civilians; that the KLA started kidnapping, establishing check-points and roadblocks. He will say that their crimes became more radical and the police were especially at risk of being kidnapped and murdered. He will tell you that the KLA opened fire on anything Serb, especially police related, but they also attacked civilians. The MUP will tell you -- the MUP officers will tell you that after the -- after the murder of a Serbian police officer in March 1998, the police could not enter Jablanica and areas under Haradinaj's control. They will tell you the police would come under fire if they attempted to enter these villages. He will tell you that the area around Lake Radonjic, and in particular the area in which the bodies were found, was a no-go area for the police. Now, in determining whether an armed conflict exists, one of the things the Trial Chamber is entitled to look at is Security Council Resolutions. There was one such very important Security Council Resolution; it was passed as early as 31st of March, 1998, and it refers to both sides of the conflict. And the part I take the Court to now says: "Condemning the use of excessive force by Serbian police forces against civilians and peaceful demonstrators in Kosovo, as well as all acts of terrorism by the Kosovo Liberation Army or any other group or individual and all external support for terrorist activity in Kosovo, including finance ... and training." The highly respected international humanitarian organisation Human Rights Watch also documented violations of the rules of war by both sides in the conflict during the indictment period. In its report, Humanitarian Law Violations in Kosovo, published in October 1998 - and this is page 3 in the summary - in a section called "Violations of the Rules of War by the KLA," it said: "The Albanian insurgency, known as the Kosovo Liberation Army/KLA, has also violated the laws of war by such actions as the taking of civilian hostages and by summary executions. Although on a lesser scale than the government abuses, these too are violations of international standards and should be condemned." The Prosecution will bring evidence from a senior Human Rights Watch monitor who was on the ground in Kosovo and will give the Court direct, first-hand evidence of what he saw and what he heard. It was also at this time, in October 1998, when Human Rights Watch was publishing its report on violations of international humanitarian law, that the KLA issued its own communique in which it confirmed there had been clashes from as early as February that year, in a communication, a communique, issued on the 17th of October, entitled "UCK Sends Memorandum to International Community," it said at the bottom -- at the very bottom of the page: "After the Serbian massacres of the Albanian population in Likoshan, Qirez, and Prekaz, in February this year, a bitter and unequal war began in Kosovo between the Serbian military, police, and paramilitary forces on one hand and the Albanian people on the other." Human Rights Watch, so concerned was it by what was occurring in Kosovo by both sides that it issued a warning. At page 75 of its report entitled "Violations of the Rules of War by the UCK," KLA," it warned the KLA that: "The rules of internal armed conflict outlined in Common Article 3 and Protocol II of the Geneva Conventions are binding on both governments and armed insurgents. As such, the UCK is legally obliged to respect the provisions of international humanitarian law, such as the protection of non-combatants and the prohibition of hostage-taking." It goes on making findings, based on its observations in the ground, based on talking to people, seeing refugees, visiting areas under attack by the KLA, the areas under siege, it said: "Despite these obligations, the UCK," that's the KLA, "has committed violations of international humanitarian law, including the taking of hostages and, by their own apparent admission, summary executions. At least 138 individuals, mostly ethnic Serbs, but also ethnic Albanians and Roma, are feared abducted by UCK." And underneath that it said: "Some UCK operations were apparently intended to drive ethnic Serbs out of their villages. Human Rights Watch heard credible reports of ethnic Serbs being forced to leave the villages of Jelovac, Kijevo, Gornji Ratis, Dasinovac, and others." Some of those are relevant to this indictment. "In a number of cases elderly Serbs refuse to leave, either too old to flee, or abandon their homes. Some of these people are currently missing and feared dead." Well, some of these people who were currently feared missing and feared dead then are the subject of this indictment. They went on: "The UCK has attacked and seized some ethnic Albanians and Roma whom it considered collaborators with the Yugoslav government." The concern of Human Rights Watch was that the UCK had issued a warning on the 12th of July, 1998 - that's at page 76 of the report - in which it had said: "First of all, all Serbian forces, whether the police, the military, or armed civilians, are our enemy. From the start, we had our own internal rules for our operations. These clearly laid down that the UCK recognises the Geneva Conventions and the conventions governing the conduct of war, even though it has not been offered the chance of signing them as it would have done. We did not go in for kidnapping, but even if some people have suffered, these have been more Albanian collaborators than Serbian civilians." As a result of that and what it saw, at page 11 of the report, Human Rights Watch issued recommendations to the KLA, calling on it to respect its obligations under international humanitarian law, to release all civilians in detention, refrain from attacks on the civilian population, and from using any detainees or civilians as hostages, and to treat humanely Serbian soldiers or policemen in custody. It also condemned hostage-taking and the ill-treatment of civilians. And it recommended the UCK to impose a code of military conduct punishing hostage-taking and breaches of international humanitarian law, and to bring to -- and to make accountable any violators. Now, I will emphasise the Limaj Trial Chamber did not have to make any findings about the existence of an armed conflict before the end of May 1998. The joint criminal enterprise pleaded in that case was pleaded to have come into existence before May 1998 and continued until at least -- until August 1998. The joint criminal enterprise pleaded in the Haradinaj case goes back earlier. The one incident -- there's an incident which stands out from many of the others pleaded in the indictment and referred to in our pre-trial brief, which goes to the mens rea of the three accused and their actus reus, the modus operandi of the KLA and the way they carried out their joint criminal enterprise. It concerned an incident on the 11th of August, 1998, in which two European Community monitors -- monitors were abducted and held -- briefly held by the KLA in Rznic, which was the village controlled by Balaj's Black Eagles. As the Court is aware, the European Community sent monitors into conflict zones during the wars in the Balkans. They were diplomatic officials and they were supposed to travel with diplomatic immunity throughout conflict areas to observe and to report and to monitor what was going on between the two sides -- the warring sides. On the 11th of August, two of them, with an Albanian interpreter and a third passenger, drove into Rznic, which was then under the control of Balaj. It was under shelling attack from Serbian forces. When they reached Rznic, they were stopped by armed KLA soldiers who demanded to know who they were and what they were doing there. The KLA soldiers pointed their guns at these diplomats and shouted at them, "Where is the international community?" In keeping with the modus operandi, they accused one of the monitors of being a Serbian spy. They ordered them to leave. But before they could leave, Balaj -- Idriz Balaj arrived with two other soldiers in a jeep and ordered the monitors to follow them to a house in Rznic, which was the local KLA headquarters. Balaj regarded the Albanian interpreter as a collaborator because he was with the person who was supposed to be a Serbian spy, that is, an ECMM monitor, and in front of these diplomats, these monitors, Balaj kicked and punched the interpreter, calling him a traitor and telling him he was going to kill him while pointing a pistol at him. Balaj took the monitors and the Albanians and the interpreter upstairs and interrogated them, again threatening to kill the interpreter. About ten minutes later Haradinaj himself arrived, and he, Haradinaj, continued the interrogation of the three in the upstairs room in KLA headquarters. Haradinaj was speaking in fluent English and fluent French to them. Haradinaj eventually took them down to the jeep. Haradinaj personally searched the diplomats' vehicle, diplomatic property, but let them leave. But importantly, during the interrogation, Haradinaj told the monitors that he, Haradinaj, was in charge of the area and no one got out of the area without his knowledge or approval. One of the monitors will testify in this court. He will describe what happened. He will describe the way the KLA members there reacted and -- reacted to and respected Haradinaj. He will describe how they saluted Haradinaj with the Albanian clenched-fist salute. He will show -- he will testify that Haradinaj was clearly in charge. He will also say, he will tell the Court, how he recognised Brahimaj as one of those present during the detention in the compound. He will describe Haradinaj as a clever and controlled person whose orders were obeyed straight away, without discussion. He will describe Haradinaj as a man who had total control of the KLA members at the compound, and that total control extended to the liberty or otherwise of the KLA -- sorry, of the ECMM monitors. I note the time. It's a quarter to 4.00. Is that an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To assist the Trial Chamber, we've prepared two large charts. They're displayed electronically and blown up in a very large proportion, and they will be available throughout the trial to assist the Trial Chamber. The first one, on the top, is an overhead, high-resolution satellite photograph showing the lake and all the relevant areas in the indictment. Underneath that is a photograph of -- on the ground, just underneath that, is a photograph showing the plotting where all the bodies were found alongside the lake. To assist the Trial Chamber, I just want to, first of all, blow up the portion on the satellite photograph to show you where each of the things you'll be hearing about in the trial are. You can see the Haradinaj house, the village of Glodjane, Rznic, the Ekonomija farm, the concrete canal, Dasinovac, and so on. You will also see at the scale -- if I can just move over for one second. There's a scale of 10 kilometres from left to about one-third of the way through which shows the Trial Chamber the scale we're talking about. To make it even more visually interesting, we have a display, a photographic display, of the various sites which you'll be hearing about and which I'll refer soon when addressing you on the evidence in relation to the bodies. What you see on the screen at the moment is basically an overhead map of the Dukagjin Zone, with Lake Radonjic in the bottom centre. If you can start with the one labeled A. The first one you can see is on the village of Rznic, and that is the junction on the road to Glodjane. The road to Glodjane is the road on the right, which goes off towards the right, and you'll see a mosque above the top. That is in Rznic and that is where the KLA -- sorry, where the ECMM monitor will tell the Court that they were stopped. There was a KLA check-point right in the middle of that junction. The next one, if we go to B, is an overhead satellite shot showing the Ekonomija farm in the top right, the KLA headquarters -- not yet, go back. In the top right is the Ekonomija farm, and you can see the canal which is very close to it. Underneath that, at the bottom of that road, is the KLA headquarters, as they then there. Just go back. At the bottom -- the bottom box, which was there a second ago, is the Haradinaj house, and that's the village of Glodjane. First of all, I'll show you the Haradinaj house. If we go back, we'll next go to the Ekonomija farm -- sorry, the KLA headquarters. That's right. That is as they are now. They didn't look like that in 1998. The next one is the Ekonomija farm, the ruins of the Ekonomija farm. Go in. If you look at the photo which is now on the screen, you'll see there's a road, and the road which -- go back. The road which intersects the two farm buildings goes directly towards the village of Rznic. The distance is about between 1 and 2 kilometres, and to the right of that you'll see a canyon on the canal. Okay. Go to the road. And that's a shot showing you directly down the road, panning around, taken in the middle of the Ekonomija farm. Okay. Thank you. I'll now take you to -- I'll now take you to the canal. You can see two highlighted areas. Go to that one, yes. Highlight that one. Again, that shows the road. Go back. And that shows the canal area and that shows the concrete -- the concrete canal area, looking in the direction of the lake, of the canal flowing from Rznic village. Go back. Go back. The next one I take you to is of Jablanica. There are two -- there's an overhead shot of Jablanica. The photo I show is the actual village of Jablanica. It's a panned shot which reveals at the bottom right there - stop - the Brahimaj house and KLA headquarters. Just go back a little bit. And if you just stop it here. If you look at the top of the photograph, in that direction you'll see the Jablanica -- where the detention centre was. Go back. Next one. The next one shows a shot of the Jablanica detention centre. This is the building as it looked last year. You can see it panning around, and we're coming to a gate. Just stop it there. The gate shows the road; to the left of the road, it goes down to Jablanica, about 1 kilometre or so away. Keep panning. Stop there. You can see on the shot in front of you at the moment, that's the door to the ruined Jablanica detention centre - pan around - that's the building as it looks now, which was the offices, and underneath is the basement where the prisoners were kept. And this shows it - photographs taken in August of last year - containing water, as witnesses will testify, similar to the condition of it in 1998. I want to take the Trial Chamber in some detail in relation to the bodies which were found along the canal, and the importance of taking the Chamber to this is to show the links and the patterns between those who were last seen in KLA custody and those whose bodies were found, identified and unidentified, mingled amongst the bodies of those last seen in KLA custody. If we could just go back to the overhead satellite photograph, you can see on the photograph in relation to where Haradinaj's house is and the canal, you can see the road -- you can see the distance, the short distance, between Haradinaj's house, the concrete canal, the Ekonomija farm, and Rznic. You can see the dirt road which leads from Rznic to the canal where the bodies were found. Now, the important point to drive home is that this area was under the control of the KLA when the victims disappeared. The next photograph I'll take you to is the photograph on which we have plotted where the bodies were found. That's a large -- that's the large photograph which is in the courtroom at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, it certainly would assist me if you'd first point at the map what place you'll take us to, and then show what the -- yes, we had it so splendidly on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. The area I'm taking Your Honours to is the canal area between Rznic and where it's labeled "Concrete Canal" and the Ekonomija farm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My finger is on the map here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And this is the area, where my hands are, which I'm demonstrating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And it's a shot taken from the Rznic overhead looking towards the canal, where the concrete part is, going down the cascades to the natural area, the canyons, to what's called the delta area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at the distance, we see the lake. Is that a lake?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the lake. The distance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the -- the photograph down. At the very top of it, is that --
