utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I ask, Your Honours, to have the e-court system on the monitoring screen for the purposes of this address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you should have a map of the region showing at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw already a map. It is a bit -- now it's there again. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just give me one moment. Your Honours, as the Prosecutor herself acknowledged in her opening address, the indictment in this case is different in a number of respects from indictments which are more usually tried by this Tribunal. There is no allegation of a mass killing or the widespread destruction of homes and properties. The indictment is in reality little more than a patchwork of individual allegations against Mr. Haradinaj's co-accused, tenuously stitched together with the evidence of a tiny handful of witnesses - no more than three or four in number - who claim to have seen Ramush Haradinaj present at the commission of particular alleged crimes. Each of those witnesses is, we say, unreliable, demonstrably so, and the evidence that they are proposing to give against Mr. Haradinaj is false. Those counts aside, the Prosecution case against Ramush Haradinaj depends on an alleged joint criminal enterprise. In order to expose the fallacy of this allegation, it is going to be necessary to analyse in some detail in the course of this trial the formation and evolution of the Kosovo Liberation Army in western Kosovo, set against the aims and objectives of the Serbian forces operating in the region. The Prosecutor urged you to pay close attention to the geography; we respectfully agree. But may we also urge you, from the outset, to pay close attention to the chronology. And I'm going to say something about each of these topics in my opening remarks. Your Honours, the indictment relates to the period during 1998 when the Kosovo Liberation Army was struggling to establish itself. During the first half of 1998, the KLA was made up of a small number of committed fighters, like Ramush Haradinaj, together with a larger number of ill-equipped and untrained volunteers. The important point is that its structure was essentially horizontal and not vertical. And that is, no doubt, why the Prosecution has not charged Mr. Haradinaj with command responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute. At this point in its history, the KLA lacked a formal or effective command structure. Most of those who fought with the KLA were villagers who would return to their daily lives when they were not actively involved in the fighting. And Mr. Haradinaj was in reality the commander of those who chose to follow him on any particular day. Given this reality, the Prosecution has been driven to resort to the vaguest possible allegation of joint criminal enterprise, effectively alleging that Mr. Haradinaj should be held responsible for the acts of all armed Kosovo Albanians in the Dukagjin region, from the very beginning of the indictment period, on the basis that he must have been party to some sort of implied agreement to commit war crimes in order to secure and maintain control of territory. Your Honours, there is no evidence at all for the existence of any such agreement. For the Prosecution to argue that Mr. Haradinaj should now be held responsible for any and every wrongful act committed within the Dukagjin region between March and September 1998 would stretch the concept of joint criminal enterprise beyond breaking point; it would render it meaningless. There was no criminal conspiracy. The objectives of the KLA in western Kosovo were to protect the local population against Serbian aggression and to fight for an independent and liberated Kosovo. As the Prosecutor herself alluded to, their cause has now been recognised by the international community, as this trial is opening. Negotiations over the future of Kosovo are well advanced. The recommendation of the UN Special Envoy for Supervised Statehood is before the Security Council, and Kosovo is widely acknowledged to be very close to achieving independence. But, Your Honours, this process has necessarily taken place in the absence of one of Kosovo's most effective politicians, a man who was widely seen as a unifying influence and the standard-bearer for his nation's hopes of independence from Serbia. And I want at the moment, and just at the outset, to say a few short words about Ramush Haradinaj as a politician and as a soldier. As president of the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo, the AAK, Mr. Haradinaj entered into a coalition government in 2004 with the Democratic League of Kosovo, the LDK, which was led by the pacifist President of Kosovo, Ibrahim Rugova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I remember that the Prosecutor said that the present political developments were not to be linked --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that we'll concentrate on the evidence of this case. So therefore, I wonder what the relevance is of this. And I add to that that -- I told you I spent some time on opening statements and literature.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the things I found several times, but it's not primarily English law I think, but perhaps Mr. Guy-Smith could guide you, that to tell already in advance whether the witnesses will be lying or not, is -- and you said these were false witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- IS supposed not to be appropriate during an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Certainly not a rule I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith is nodding yes. So, you see, the convergence of the several systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, relevance on this matter, Mr. Haradinaj, especially since Mr. Guy-Smith expressed his concern that it would become a political statement, whereas Madam Del Ponte, I would say, only said that it had nothing to do with politics. And this Chamber also considers this case to be a case in which it has to be established whether the accused committed -- is responsible for any of the crimes in the indictment. So, therefore, if you'd please limit yourself in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I simply say this: The relevance of this part of what I wanted to say - and it's very brief - is in relation to Ramush Haradinaj's attitude to minority populations within Kosovo, which is one of the issues that the Tribunal is going to have to look into. And one of the distinguishing features of Mr. Haradinaj as a political leader was his commitment to the protection and integration of Kosovo's ethnic minority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's in later stages, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In later stages, and Your Honours will need to see the history, if I may say so, in its context, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The message is received clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We say, Your Honours, that it is essentially that feature which, perhaps more than any other, made him such a threat to those who opposed independence for Kosovo. And as Your Honours know, as soon as the indictment in this case was issued, Mr. Haradinaj announced his resignation as Prime Minister, immediately travelled to The Hague to surrender himself. And in his resignation speech, he urged the government to continue to be guided by the rules of mutual tolerance, respect for the rule of law, and support for minority ethnic communities. May I simply draw Your Honours' attention to this short extract from a report published at the time by the International Crisis Group, Mr. Haradinaj it says: "... expressed appreciation for the partnership of the UN Secretary-General's special representative and the commander of the international troops (COMKFOR), thereby helping to shield the international presence ... from potential back-lash. His last government meeting was with Serb and Bosniak ministers, at which he stressed that there would be no attacks on minority Serbs. Crucially he relayed a pointed message to people on the ground not to make trouble ... The message given by Haradinaj from the moment of his indictment was to stay focussed on the big picture and keep faith with the institutional route to statehood." And that is a position that he has consistently maintained during his period of provisional release. Your Honour, that is all I want to say at this stage about Ramush Haradinaj, the politician. But may I turn then for a moment to Ramush Haradinaj, the soldier. Mr. Haradinaj fought an honourable war. His targets were combatants, not civilians. And faced with the overwhelming fire-power of the combined Serbian forces, he sought to organise the defence of the Albanian population in the area around Glodjane. He led by example. He never expected KLA volunteers to fight battles he was not prepared to fight himself. And he had no time for armchair generals who claimed political leadership but who made little or no active contribution to the armed struggle against Serbia. In those respects, he was undoubtedly a tough and independent fighter, and an effective one. But the targeting of Serb civilians, or any civilians, was never one of Mr. Haradinaj's military objectives, and he never ordered or condoned the ill-treatment of detainees. That sort of dishonourable conduct is the very opposite of the principles which have guided Ramush Haradinaj, both as a soldier and as a politician. I would like, if I may, briefly to sketch in the essential military facts, political and military facts, which are relevant to this indictment to put it in its context. Your Honours, Kosovo has rightly been described as the book ends of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. In the second half of the 1980s, the Serbian leadership under Slobodan Milosevic began making plans for the creation of a Greater Serbia, a centralised Serbian state, encompassing the Serb-populated areas of Croatia and Bosnia, and it would include the whole of Kosovo, considered by many Serbs to be their cultural heartland and the cradle of the Serbian Orthodox Church. The twin objectives for Kosovo, so far as the Belgrade regime was concerned, were to implement constitutional changes which would deprive Kosovo of its autonomous status under the constitution and to modify the ethnic balance in Kosovo through a policy of discrimination, repression, and ultimately ethnic cleansing. This was to be achieved in three stages: Revocation of Kosovo's autonomy under the constitution of what was then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; a decade of repression of the Albanian population; and finally, in 1998, a military crackdown on the armed Albanian resistance, which was used as a pretext for attacks on the Albanian civilian population as a whole aimed at driving them out of Kosovo. And I want, if I may, to look very briefly at the first two of those stages and then in a little more detail at the third. At the end of 1988 and the beginning of 1989, the Serbian Assembly made changes to the constitution of the fry, effectively revoking Kosovo's autonomy. Large-scale demonstrations took place throughout Kosovo, many of which were violently crushed by riot police. There were mass arrests and as many as a hundred people were killed. A year later the Serbian Assembly adopted a package of legislative measures to suppress the rights of the majority Albanian population in Kosovo, Kosovar Albanians were dismissed from political and economic institutions, Albanian property transactions were annulled, education in Albanian was suppressed, and Albanian lecturers and students were excluded from the universities. More than 80.000 Albanians were expelled from their jobs. Between 1994 and 1997, the situation in Kosovo deteriorated further. The Serbian regime became increasingly violent and repressive. Writing at the beginning of the 1998, the historian Noel Malcolm recorded the situation in these terms. He said: "To produce an adequate survey of the human rights abuses suffered by the Albanians of Kosovo since 1990 would require several long chapters in itself. Every aspect of life in Kosovo has been affected ... "Arbitrary arrest and police violence have become routine ... "Serbian law does not, of course, permit the beating up of people in police custody; but many graphic testimonies exist of severe beatings with truncheons, the application of electric shocks to the genitals, and so on ... "An overall strategy of persuading Albanians to leave by rendering their conditions of life intolerable was in operation." Your Honours, during that decade of repression, a number of Kosovo Albanian political parties emerged. The Democratic League of Kosovo, the LDK, was formed in 1989. And under the chairmanship of Ibrahim Rugova, the LDK advocated a peaceful solution of the Kosovo question through dialogue with Belgrade. The Popular Movement for Kosovo, the LPK, on the other hand, advocated a solution through active means, including, if necessary, armed insurrection. Pockets of armed resistance sprung up, but it was not until the end of 1997 that the Kosovo Liberation Army made its first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You really have to slow down a bit; because the transcriber, otherwise, will be behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll let it catch up for a moment. I think we're there, are we? No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I got to the point where I was saying it was at the back end of 1997 that the Kosovo Liberation Army made its first public appearance in Kosovo. By this time, President Milosevic and his supporters had resolved to take the next step in their plan for Kosovo, by destroying those Albanian villages that were perceived to be the heartland of armed resistance to the Serb regime. And so at the beginning of 1998, orders were issued to implement this plan and to arm the Serb civilian population of Kosovo. Your Honours, the first Serbian attacks occurred in late February and early March of 1998. And it might be helpful just to look at the geography for a moment, to mark in the main towns in Kosovo, we have, Prishtine, the capital; Peje in the west; Gjakove on the southern edge of the Dukagjin region; Kline, on the eastern edge of the Dukagjin region; Prizren in the south; and Ferizaj on the south eastern border of Kosovo. On 28th February, 1998, Serb forces launched an attack on two villages in the Drenica region: Qirez and Likoshan. They attacked without warning, firing indiscriminately at civilians. Helicopters, armoured military vehicles, mortars and machine-guns were used. And by the end of the day, 26 Albanians, including a pregnant woman, had been killed, many of them at close range. At least 12 of these people were put to death after they had been arrested. On the 5th of March, nine years ago today, Serb forces attacked the family compound of a KLA leader called Adem Jashari in Prekaz. This is an event that has considerable significance for Kosovar Albanians. Police special forces shelled the Jashari family compound and then shot all those who survived. 58 people were killed, including 18 women and 10 children under the age of 16. At about the same time, an attack was launched on the nearby village of Laushe. In all, more than 80 Kosovar Albanians were killed in those brutal operations, including women, young children and the elderly. Your Honour, that is the background to what took place on the 24th of March, because it was only a few weeks after those attacks, on the 24th of March, that Serb forces launched an assault on the Haradinaj family compound in Gllogjan. The male members of the Haradinaj family returned fire. On this occasion, they provided a sufficient fire cover to enable the women and children of the family to escape, and then managed to hold the Serb forces at bay until they were able to escape themselves under cover of darkness. Mr. Haradinaj was seriously injured. During the day, Serb forces were seen using heavy weapons, including the Praga 30-millimetre cannon, armoured vehicles and helicopters in Gllogjan. Paramilitary police entered the village, engaging in fire-fighting. Many people were detained. Large parts of the village were destroyed, and three teenagers were killed by Serb forces as they were fleeing to safety. Reports suggest that school children were used by the Serb forces as human shields, and one elderly couple was shelled in their home. Simultaneous attacks were launched on the nearby villages, including Irzniq. These villages were effectively left empty when the civilian population fled at that time. And that is the -- or marks what is, in effect, the first milestone in the indictment. These were, by no means, the only Serb military attacks in western Kosovo at this time. From the 24th of March onwards, Gllogjan and its surrounding villages were under almost constant attack from the Serb forces stationed on high ground just a few kilometres to the south. And around Easter 1998, a VJ tank unit attacked Decan, destroying large parts of the town. As a result of these attacks, many people - Serbs, Roma, Albanians - left the area to escape the fighting. Your Honours, the most serious and sustained Serbian attacks occurred in the course of three major offensives between May and September. These provide the principal milestones in the Serbian campaign in western Kosovo during the period covered by this indictment. The first occurred towards the end of May; the second, at the end of July and the beginning of August; and the third, from the beginning of September. I'll say a few words, if I may, about each of these, because they are essential to an understanding of the military objectives of the KLA in the Dukagjin region, and they are also essential to a proper evaluation of the Prosecution's case as to what was taking place on the ground. In the second half of May, a Serbian offensive was launched in the Dukagjin region. After a number of devastating attacks on towns and villages close to the Albanian border, Serb forces attacked a village called Grabanice on the 19th and 20th of May, killing a number of civilians and causing most of the local population to flee the area. On the 25th of May, Serb special forces attacked the villages of Lybeniq and Strellc. Buildings were burned, and 11 villagers were killed. Then on the 28th of May, Serb forces advanced southwest from Peje and launched attacks in the areas around Vranoq and Baran. Simultaneous attacks - this is the 28th of May, a day of some significance to this indictment - simultaneous attacks occurred on the same day in Junik, in Carabreg, in Prejlep, in Isniq, and in Rastavice. The pattern, Your Honours, for these attacks in each case was essentially the same. First, villages would be surrounded with heavy artillery and armoured vehicles. There would then be a destructive phase of bombardment, and then the notorious paramilitary police would enter the area on foot, shooting survivors who had remained behind, looting Albanian property, killing livestock, and setting fire to everything from buildings and schools to haystacks. These were euphemistically called "mopping up" operations. In many instances, villages were simply razed to the ground, and you will hearing in due course some evidence about that. These Serbian operations were characterised invariably by the use of indiscriminate and excessive force, with no distinction being drawn between combatants and civilians. Your Honours, throughout this period, the Serb forces were maintaining constant pressure on the villages around Gllogjan, a matter of some importance in assessing the Prosecution's central thesis about KLA control in a territory. They were regularly shelling from vantage points in elevated positions to the south, supported by paramilitary police units who made forays into the areas on the ground. The people ultimately responsible for many of these attacks, General Bozidar Delic and General Dragan Zivanovic, are witnesses the Prosecution is proposing to call. Your Honours, the second major Serbian offensive was launched across the region at the end of July and the beginning of August. The villages attacked in this phase of the campaign included Junik, Rastavice, and Prejlep. On the 2nd of August, Serb forces entered Jabllanice. Gramaqel was overrun on the 8th of August, and the villages of Shaptej and Rastavice fell to the Serbs on the 9th of August. Serb forces then moved towards Gllogjan and Irzniq, the towns of villages at the centre of this indictment, and they took control of them on the 12th of August. Your Honours, a BBC film crew was in Gllogjan and Irzniq at the time that Serb forces took control of this area and captured footage of the Serb assault. And the broadcast that I'm about to show to Your Honours gives a vivid picture of the situation on the ground. It's a short piece of film and needs to be heard through headphones on channel 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Reporter: The Serbs know that they have the upper hand and they are determined to press home the advantage. This time you've got the village of Glodjane in flames shelled and machine-gunned into submission. On the other side the KLA allowed us exclusive access to their new front line. They're nervous but determined. Some of these men come from this village. They know what's happened up ahead and they now lie directly in the path of the Serb offensive, which has already removed the rebel fighters from most of their strongholds in Kosovo. "The waiting is tense, but already it's clear that they won't have to wait long. The shells are now falling on Rznic. Against artillery there's little that the KLA has been able to do but run. All this is happening while both sides consider peace proposals and the international community struggles to find a way forward. "Despite the international diplomacy, the situation on the ground remains unchanged. The Serbs are still pressing their offensive; the KLA still defending their villages and communities. The Serbs, of course, don't see it that way. They insist that the rebel fighters are the problem, and without them so much misery and destruction could have been avoided. "Here it's the paramilitary police that are bearing down on the KLA. In other places we saw heavily armed units of the Army of Yugoslavia. The Serbs say they now regard this as a mopping-up operation. For the KLA it's becoming a battle for survival. When there is fighting there are, of course, more refugees. Almost 200.000 people have been made homeless by this conflict the aid agencies have been hoping that they would return to their villages. What's happened today makes that a very distant prospect. "Jeremy Cook, BBC news, Rznic, Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, as that footage shows, much of the civilian population of Gllogjan and Irzniq left the area. The KLA was driven out, too, and the entire area, including the area around Lake Radoniq and the canal, was left under the exclusive control of the Serbian paramilitaries. By the time the villagers began to return to their homes in Gllogjan two weeks later, the Serb forces had withdrawn. Your Honours, the last of the major Serb offensives to take place during the period covered by the indictment was launched just a few weeks later, at the beginning of September. This time Serb forces, including the VJ and the paramilitary police, engaged in coordinated attacks on ethnic Albanian villages across large swathes of Kosovo. As part of that offensive, on the 3rd of September, Serb forces attacked Gllogjan again. They approached from Gergoc to the east and from Peje and Carabreg to the west. And they left a corridor, as was common, to encourage civilians to flee towards the Albanian border. Extensive damage was inflicted on many of the villages in the area, and Serb forces were still engaged, on the Prosecution's own evidence, in burning and looting Albanian property a week after the attack. I want to turn now, if I may, to the emergence of the armed Kosovo Albanian resistance movement. The Kosovo Liberation Army, the KLA, was formed in 1994, although its existence did not, as I've said, become widely known in Kosovo until 1997. From the beginning, the KLA was a prescribed organisation and it operated underground. Between 1994 and 1997, KLA members and other armed fighters mounted a relatively small number of sporadic armed attacks on the Serb forces. Now, Mr. Haradinaj was living outside Kosovo during this period, mainly in Switzerland. He left Kosovo in 1991, and although he made a number of clandestine visits in the intervening period, he did not return to live there again until the end of February/beginning of March. At that time, and this is really central to an understanding of the way the Prosecution puts its case, at that time the KLA had no formal or organised military structure in place; it essentially consisted of small pockets of resistance in different parts of Kosovo. During the course of his opening, Mr. Re suggested that when Mr. Haradinaj arrived back in Kosovo, he was appointed immediately as commander of the Dukagjin Zone and that he was a member of the KLA General Staff. That suggestion shows, if we may say so, a surprising lack of familiarity with the Prosecution's own evidence. The Dukagjin Zone did not exist at all at that time, nor was Mr. Haradinaj, then or ever, a member of the KLA General Staff. But, Your Honour, in response to those attacks in Qirez, Likoshan, Prekaz at the end of February and the beginning of March and then Gllogjan, rudimentary village defence groups began to form and seek to organise themselves. They were, by and large, volunteers without military training. Weapons and uniforms were in short supply and attempts were made to bring supplies in from Albania. Initially, these villages were operating autonomously. But in late May, the first real attempt was made to coordinate the different village defences into a single command structure. At a meeting which Mr. Haradinaj convened in Gllogjan in the last week of May, a regional staff was established for the area. A number of subzones were set up, each led by its own commander. And at that point Mr. Haradinaj was the commander of the subzone centred around Gllogjan. The other zones which gathered together, or the other centres which gathered together, at the time of that end-of-May meeting, were centred around the village of Irzniq, where the commander was a man called Shemsedin Cekaj; Dashinoc, where the commander was a man called Rrustem Tetaj; and Irzniq, a little further to the north, which was under the joint leadership of two men called Gani Gjukaj and Skender Rexhahemetaj. It's important to emphasise that within these areas the KLA did not have exclusive control of the territory. The situation was fluid with armed engagements taking place between the KLA and the paramilitary police on a regular basis. The areas covered by these first subzones are best understood as pockets in which there was a concentration of armed Albanian resistance fighters who were loyal to the emerging KLA. It's also important to emphasise that the villages that came together at the end of May did not include villages from across the whole of what later became known as the Dukagjin Operational Zone. They did not include, for example, the KLA base at Jabllanice. However, about a month later - we're moving forward now to the 23rd of June - a decision was taken to create a single zone in Dukagjin which would include Jabllanice, to the east, and Junik, to the west. That process of amalgamation created this new larger area which was the Dukagjin Operational Zone. The Dukagjin Operational Zone came into existence on the 23rd of June, and Mr. Re, albeit very briefly, flashed before Your Honours the minutes of the meeting at which that zone was created. Ramush Haradinaj was elected by those present at the meeting to be the zone commander, and Lahi Brahimaj was elected as his deputy. But, Your Honours, within that structure - and one can see it from the way it evolved - local commanders retained a significant level of autonomy and independence. Communication existed but was rudimentary and coordination existed but was rudimentary. And local village groups and commanders would often respond spontaneously to events as they unfolded in their area, without waiting for orders from any central command. And that applied not only to defensive action aimed at protecting local civilian populations of a particular village against Serb military attacks or the attacks of Serbian paramilitary units, but also to the mounting of offensive operations against the Serb forces. There was a very significant level of local autonomy within the structure. Your Honours, put very briefly, those then are the essential military facts relevant to the present indictment. And can I turn now to the allegations made against Mr. Haradinaj in a little more detail and, nonetheless, in overview. Your Honours, of the 37 counts on the indictment, Mr. Haradinaj is alleged to have been present at, or to have participated in, a total of five of the incidents alleged. Your Honours know that those allegations are completely denied. As for the remaining 32 counts on the indictment, the Prosecution case against Mr. Haradinaj is based solely on an allegation of joint criminal enterprise with his co-accused and with others. Your Honours, we say there is simply no credible evidence of Mr. Haradinaj acting together with his co-accused or with others named as members of the alleged joint criminal enterprise in pursuit of any common criminal objectives. On inspection, the Prosecution case on joint criminal enterprise comes down to two central propositions, each of which we say is fundamentally flawed. The first proposition is that throughout the indictment period the KLA, under Ramush Haradinaj, exercised exclusive control over an area of territory to the east of the Peje-Gjakove road, which the Prosecution has called the Area of Total Control. That's why it's important to understand the reality of the military engagements on the ground. The second proposition on which the joint criminal enterprise allegation effectively rests follows on from the first. The Prosecution suggest that the Dukagjin KLA and, by implication, Mr. Haradinaj, must now be held responsible for the deaths of 31 individuals whose remains were recovered from the Lake Radoniq canal area, principally, as Mr. Re pointed out, because, says the Prosecution, those remains were found within this so-called Area of Total Control. Your Honours, the first of these propositions is inconsistent with the facts. The suggestion that the KLA had complete control of the relevant area to the exclusion of all Serb forces is unsustainable. The three major Serbian offensives that I've outlined each involved attacks by Serb forces, including Serb paramilitaries, on villages within the so-called area of total control. But, Your Honours, quite apart from those major offensives, there is indisputable evidence that Serb forces, including special forces, were operating within the area and, in some instances, were operating immediately adjacent to Lake Radoniq. Your Honours, in order to understand the geography, it might be helpful if I just briefly show Your Honours an aerial view of the canal and the lake, moving from Irzniq down towards the canal area. Your Honours, we can see in this image Irzniq to the right, bottom right hand of the screen, and the blue line traces the route of the canal. The camera is moving southwest along the canal route in the direction of the lake. You see Gllogjan just disappearing to the right. The camera is now approaching the Economic farm, and then travelling on towards the lake. Can I ask Your Honours just to note those two roads, two dirt roads, on either side of the canal and head down towards the area around the lake. Now, Your Honours, it is clear from contemporary records that Serb forces, including paramilitary units, were stationed at a number of locations in the immediate vicinity of the lake from April 1998 onwards and throughout the indictment period, and that they were conducting operations from those positions. They were based at vantage points in elevated positions just a few kilometres from Gllogjan. On the east side of the lake, there were Serb troops at Suka Cermjan. On the west side, they were stationed at Suka Bitesh and at Suka Babaloqit. These hills have different names in Serbian, but they are all marked with their relevant heights on the maps that Your Honours have. And this first slide gives a rough indication of the view from the vantage point of the Serb forces at Suka Cermjan with Gllogjan and Irzniq in the distance. Your Honours, moving a little to the west, we can see the view from the south shore of Lake Radoniq, with Suka Bitesh in the centre of the picture, and the next slide shows the vantage point at Suka Bitesh. This slide shows the vantage point from Suka Babaloqit, again with Gllogjan marked on the map. Just as a rough indication, Gllogjan is approximately equidistant between Suka Bitesh and the canal area. It's important, if I may, to emphasise that each of these hills is less than 4 kilometres from Gllogjan, the closest approximately 3 kilometres. So the theory that lies at the heart of the Prosecution's case that during the indictment period, the KLA exercised total and effective control of the area to the east of the Peje-Gjakove road, to the exclusion of Serb forces, is simply wrong. Your Honours, this last view shows the view from the north side of the canal looking south towards the Economic farm, and those two hills of Serb forces in the background. Gllogjan can be seen to the right of the picture. And if, Your Honours, if I can just direct your attention for a moment to the blue line running along the canal. If you can see the point where the blue line turns to white, that shows the approximate position at which the Serbian authorities recorded the discovery of human remains in September 1998, which brings me to the second limb of the Prosecution case on joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, in total, 31 sets of human remains were recovered by Serbian forensic teams, or were recorded as having been recovered, in that area in early September. It is common ground that these individuals died on different dates over a six-month period and that the discovery of their remains does not imply any sort of mass killing or collective execution. Nonetheless, the Prosecution seeks to argue that all of the remains distributed along the canal area must be victims of crimes committed by the KLA primarily because they were recovered within the so-called area of total control. We submit that approach is fundamentally misconceived. It is important, if I may say so, to emphasise that of the 31 sets of remains recovered in the area, eight are still [sic] Identified, and there are a further ten sets of remains that have been identified by DNA but for whom there is no evidence as to the circumstances of their death. Would Your Honours give me a moment. I think there's an error on the transcript. Eight unidentified. In respect, Your Honours, of both the unidentified and the unattributed remains, there is no evidence to suggest that they were killed by members of the KLA, still less that their deaths were war crimes; that the plain fact is that no one knows how they died or who killed them. In addition to those 20 sets of remains, there are four further sets of remains for which there is no DNA analysis. And as we've explained in our pre-trial brief, the -- what are called the traditional methods of identification, clothing identification, essentially, compared -- together with a comparison of pre-and post mortem data, those traditional methods of identification which were used by the Serbian forensic teams have yielded a 50 per cent rate of error in identification on the facts of this case. And they, for that reason, we would respectfully submit, are to be disregarded as unreliable bases for inferring identification. Your Honour, in the absence of DNA evidence, there is no safe basis for establishing the identity of these individuals. And in the absence of reliable evidence as to their identity, there is no means of reliably establishing the circumstances in which they met their deaths. Your Honours, drawing the various threads together, the resulting position is this: Of the 31 sets of remains recorded by the Serb forensic teams, there are nine individuals identified by DNA in respect of whom the Prosecution intends to call evidence alleging KLA responsibility for their deaths in one form or another; essentially, in many cases, evidence that they were detained. Now, obviously - and I don't propose to comment on it - but the reliability of that evidence is an issue for Your Honours to determine in the trial, and it is in dispute. But it is, nonetheless, worth pointing out at this early stage of the trial, on Mr. Haradinaj's behalf, that those nine individuals are named as the victims of five pairs of counts on the indictment, none of which alleges the presence or direct participation of Mr. Haradinaj. But, Your Honours, the flaws in the Prosecution case in relation to the canal are not brought to an end by that recognition. There are, we say, serious grounds to question the integrity of the Serbian recovery operation as a whole, which are going to need to be explored in some detail in the trial. There are a number of indications to suggest that the alleged crime scene may well have been manipulated for propaganda purposes. There are questions relating not only to the canal area itself but also to six further sets of remains that were allegedly recovered at or about the same time, at the nearby Economic farm. Mr. Re made no mention of those six people, and for good reason. They are no longer included in the indictment. That is because the Prosecution now recognises that they were, in all probability, or may well have been, killed by Serb forces. Indeed, Your Honours, the family of three of those victims have told the Prosecution that they last saw their relatives alive in Serb custody. All six of those victims were Albanian. They all had family connections to the KLA. And one of them was related to the Jashari family, who had been the target of the massacre in Prekaz in early March. But, Your Honours, the removal of those charges from the indictment doesn't mean that these six bodies are irrelevant to the present case. The remains of those six individuals had been deliberately placed at the Economic farm by someone. The official claims made by the Serbian authorities, including those involved in the forensic evidence that you are going to hear, that they were victims of the KLA and must have been, points, we say, to an orchestrated attempt to manipulate the evidence in order to hide the responsibility of Serb forces for those deaths, and at the same time falsely to implicate the KLA. If that is, indeed, what happened in this case, then it would not be the only occasion on which Serb forces had engaged in the falsification of evidence and the transportation of bodies. In the Milutinovic case, for example, the Prosecution itself alleges that Serb forces removed and transported the bodies of Kosovar Albanian victims in order to escape responsibility for their crimes. And the Prosecution also alleges that the Serb forces were ordered to carry a quantity of Chinese ammunition so that they could falsely implicate the KLA in crimes that had been committed by Serb special forces. That, too, has an echo in the present case. The presence of Chinese ammunition in the Lake Radoniq canal area was specifically highlighted by the Serb authorities, and, indeed, by the Prosecution in its pre-trial brief, as evidence of KLA responsibility. The Serb authorities pointed, in particular, to the finding of Chinese ammunition when presenting their findings to the media and to representatives of the international community. So, Your Honours, we say it is impossible to draw any safe conclusions from the precise location in which the various human remains are said to have been found by the Serbian authorities involved in this recovery operation. The photograph you were shown with the positions marked on it - we can see it there at the bottom - that is produced by the Prosecution based on records provided by those directly involved in the Serbian recovery operation which resulted in the claim that six people at the Economic farm were KLA victims, and must have been. It was not, as one might have had the impression, an analysis conducted with impartiality or by independents or internationals. And, Your Honours, once there is evidence suggesting manipulation and fabrication of material at the crime scene, it becomes impossible, we say, to have any confidence in the integrity of the crime scene evidence. Your Honours, I want to turn now to the counts alleging crimes against humanity, but briefly. On this aspect of the case, the Defence places considerable reliance on the findings of the Trial Chamber in the Limaj case. In that case, the Trial Chamber found that the evidence did not establish, or even indicate, that the KLA had a policy of targeting civilians as such, whether Serbian or Kosovar Albanian. Your Honours, it's important that I emphasise four points about this aspect of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you one question, Mr. Emmerson. When we talk about findings of Trial Chambers --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- especially when there's still an appeal pending, I take it, then, that sooner or later you'll discuss with Mr. Re whether or not it would be appropriate to make any application for taking judicial notice of -- and then of course it should qualify. Do I understand this presentation to be that, if need be, that there will be an application for taking judicial notice? Because, of course, with due respect, what other Trial Chambers have decided is, I wouldn't say irrelevant, but it's not on the basis of the evidence which is before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There are, if I may say so, four points that I want in particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- which tackle the issue that Your Honour has just raised. The first point is that the findings of the Limaj Trial Chamber were not, as Mr. Re suggested, confined to any particular region of Kosovo. They were expressed as applying to the whole of Kosovo. The second point is that the principal evidence which the Prosecution relies on in this case was also before the Trial Chamber in Limaj. The Chamber had heard evidence relating to the discovery of human remains at the Lake Radoniq canal area and in relation to the alleged ill-treatment of detainees at Jabllanice. And third, while Your Honour is right to say that there's an appeal pending, the Prosecution has not appealed this aspect of the findings in Limaj. There is no appeal in relation to crimes against humanity. And fourthly, the Prosecution has made no attempt, in its pre-trial brief or in its opening, to explain how the findings in Limaj can properly be distinguished in the present case. And, Your Honour, we say - and this really answers Your Honour's question - that the conclusions reached by the Limaj Trial Chamber, whether they're binding is not the point; they are right. And they are borne out by the evidence in the present case. Your Honours, the actual counts on this indictment allege the deaths of a total of 12 Serbs across the Dukagjin region over a period of approximately six months. 12 Serbs across the period of six months across the Dukagjin region. And in respect of six of those individuals, there is no evidence at all as to the circumstances of their death, which must therefore remain a matter of speculation. There are six Serb individuals on the indictment in respect of whom the Prosecution proposes to call evidence alleging direct KLA responsibility in one form or another. Your Honour, the very last main topic I want to address, and very briefly indeed, is the date on which a state of armed conflict can properly be said to have come into existence in Kosovo. That is obviously something which raises a jurisdictional issue which may affect, in particular, those counts which are alleged to have occurred in the early months of the indictment period. Your Honour, it is sufficient at this point for me to say that the Trial Chamber's judgement in Limaj strongly suggests that the operative date would be sometime towards the end of May. That was, as it happens, the date that the Prosecution's own expert witness put on it when advanced as evidence in that case. It is, of course, ultimately for the Prosecution to prove when, during the period covered by the present indictment, a state of internal armed conflict can properly be said to have come into existence. Polemic and rhetoric, even the comments of international human rights groups as to whether a state of armed conflict was in existence at a particular time, are of marginal value. It's a matter, we say, for the Trial Chamber to evaluate, properly applying the law to the facts and the evidence. And the arguments of the Defence are fully set out in our pre-trial brief and will be developed at a later stage of this case. Your Honours, in conclusion, may I say this: For the people of Kosovo, the conflict in 1998 and 1999 was, very obviously, a brutal and overwhelming experience. Best estimates suggest that 12.000 people died, 120.000 homes were destroyed, countless women were raped by Serb forces, and at one point a million people were displaced from a population of only 2 million. During 1998, the KLA in the Dukagjin region was facing some of the most ruthless forces of the Serbian regime. For the KLA and for Ramush Haradinaj, lives depended on making the right decisions every hour of every day. And as the BBC reporter we saw earlier put it, they were fighting to defend their villages and communities and it was, for them, a struggle of survival. The people of western Kosovo would not have supported the KLA, would not have fed them and sheltered them and tended to their wounds, if they had behaved in the way that the Prosecution alleges in this case. Your Honours, there was no agreement to commit war crimes. There was no agreement to persecute or kill civilians or ill-treat detainees. Ramush Haradinaj is not a war criminal. The charges against him are completely unfounded, and the Prosecutor's decision to indict him was unjust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Since none of the other counsel have announced any wish to make an opening statement, and since none of the accused wants to apply for an unsworn statement under Rule 84 bis, this concludes the delivery of the opening statements. There are a few practical and technical matters I'd like to raise. Some of them will have to be dealt with in private session, but the first one I'll deal with in open session, and that's the following: Today some videos were played. The video played by the Prosecution was a silent one, without any spoken text, from what I remember, Mr. Re, if I'm remembering well. That was different with the video played where the comment was in English which does not appear at this moment at the transcript, which most likely - but I didn't check that - means that it will not appear on the French transcript either. Therefore, we have to find a solution for that. I suggest to the parties that we -- in order to have as complete a record as possible, that we deal with videos in the following manner: That the parties provide to the interpreters' booth a transcript of the spoken words in the original language; that then this will be read out so that it will be transcribed for the English transcript. At the same time, the text is very often spoken, even if it's not read out, if it's at least transcribed so that it appears on the English transcript. At the same time, sometimes the text is spoken so quickly that it's impossible for the interpreters to translate it so that it also appears on the French transcript. A solution to that would be if one of the interpreters would read the transcript provided by the party and checks whether what the interpreter reads is the same as what the interpreter hears, and that the other interpreter then interprets the text on the basis of the transcript, since there's a fair chance that the interpreter would not be able to follow at the speed of the spoken words. This would guarantee that we have complete transcripts both in English and in French, and also that working on the basis of the transcript is verified as to whether the transcript reflects the original spoken words. This is a suggestion to the parties and to the interpreters' booth. We practiced this same technique in one of the other cases I presided over. It is a burden; at the same time, it worked well and it avoids a lot of -- it avoids errors made. At the same time, Mr. Emmerson, I remember that you said when the video was introduced that we had to put on our earphones because that's how we could follow the text. You certainly remember that at a recent meeting, it was requested that everyone always uses his earphones in order to hear also comments by the interpreters, such as: "Could you please slow down," et cetera. So, therefore, everyone is encouraged to follow that suggestion and not the suggestion made by you only to put on your earphones if it's needed to hear the video. Then these were the technical matters we could deal with in open session. Before we adjourn, I'd like to go into private session, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber is aware, Mr. Re, that where we hurried you up a bit, that we would have left seven minutes, which might have diminished a bit of the pressure upon you to finish your opening statement. But that's reality, let's say it this way. Unless there's any other procedural issue to be raised at this moment. Mr. Guy-Smith, I see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I thought it might be of some assistance, because an issue had come up with regard to some language that was used in something that I was reading during the Prosecution's presentation on the ELMO, so it was information that was produced by the Prosecution, if perhaps we obtained a full file of the Sanctions and the slides that were used during the presentation of the Prosecution's opening statement, it might be of assistance in also having a complete record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's a very, very innocent explanation for this. The document which was displayed was the official translation, and the one I was reading from was the draft translation. And when I put mine to mind, it was just -- it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith was asking for a complete record. Would you be able to provide whatever you used to the Defence? I don't think it will take a major effort. Anything else? If not, then we'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2. Madam Registrar, I take it the same courtroom? Not this same courtroom. Courtroom II, tomorrow, quarter past 2. We'll then hear the witness next called and we'll deal with a few procedural matters in the beginning of the next session. We stand adjourned.
